stages.name: Fiscal deficits and national debt
stages.title: Fiscal deficits and national debt
stages.sub: How the ups and downs of the economy feed into government borrowing, and why a deficit is not the same as debt.

steps.q: Over several years, a country's output grows fast, then slows, then shrinks a little, then grows fast again, on repeat. What does this pattern of ups and downs describe?
steps.right: Regular swings between growth and slowdown
steps.wrong: A one-off change that then stays fixed
steps.hint: Think about whether the economy keeps repeating booms and slowdowns, or settles once and for all.

steps.q: In a slowdown, more people lose their jobs and claim benefits automatically, without any new law being passed. In a boom, more people earn and pay tax automatically, without any new law. Does government spending and tax revenue change on their own as the cycle moves, even if no policy is changed?
steps.right: Yes, they change automatically with the cycle
steps.wrong: No, they only change if a new policy is passed
steps.hint: Compare this to discretionary fiscal policy, where the government deliberately changes tax or spending. Is anyone deciding anything here?

steps.q: In a recession year, benefit payments rise and tax revenue falls, so the government spends £80bn but only collects £70bn in that same year. What is the £10bn gap between spending and revenue in that one year called?
steps.right: A shortfall the government must borrow to cover that year
steps.wrong: The total amount the government owes from all past years
steps.hint: Focus on just this one year's spending compared with this one year's revenue.

steps.q: The government runs a deficit and borrows £10bn this year, on top of all the money it has already borrowed and not yet repaid from previous years. What do we call the total amount still owed, built up from every year's borrowing?
steps.right: The total stock of past borrowing still owed
steps.wrong: The amount borrowed in this one year alone
steps.hint: This is not just this year's gap, it is everything ever borrowed and not yet paid back.

steps.q: If the government eliminates this year's deficit completely by balancing spending and revenue, does the pile of past borrowing still owed disappear immediately too?
steps.right: No, it stays until it is actually repaid
steps.wrong: Yes, it clears as soon as the deficit is closed
steps.hint: One is what happens in a single year, the other has built up over many years. Does fixing one year's gap wipe out everything owed from before?
